summary: RFC 8954 limited the size of the optional Nonce extension in the Online Certificate Status Protocol, which binds a response to a particular request. Some environments use algorithms that produce longer nonce values. This document obsoletes RFC 8954, replacing its Nonce size limit so nonces can be longer than 32 octets.

plainLanguage.summary: When you ask whether an ID card is still valid, you include a secret number so the answer cannot be a replay of an old one. This lets that secret number be longer when needed.

subtitle: Lets the OCSP Nonce be up to 128 octets long, while telling clients to use at least 32.

tldr.problem: RFC 8954 capped the OCSP Nonce at 32 octets, but some environments use cryptographic algorithms that generate longer nonce values.
tldr.mechanism: This document raises the maximum Nonce length to 128 octets, keeps a 1 octet minimum for old clients, and requires new requesters to send at least 32 octets.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 8954 and updates RFC 6960. Implementations that follow only RFC 8954 cannot process nonces longer than 32 octets.

today: RFC 9654 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 8954 and updates RFC 6960, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why the Nonce Limit Changed
sections.content:
The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) is used to check the status of a certificate. Its optional Nonce extension, first defined in Section 4.4.1 of RFC 6960, cryptographically binds an OCSP response to a particular request. That guarantees the response is fresh and avoids replay attacks.

RFC 8954 limited the Nonce to a maximum of 32 octets. Some environments use cryptographic algorithms that generate longer values. This document raises the maximum to 128 octets, and recommends that requesters and responders use a Nonce of at least 32 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule said the secret number could only be so long. Some people needed a longer one, so the rule now allows a much longer number.

sections.title: The Nonce Extension
sections.content:
The Nonce is carried as one of the requestExtensions in a request and as one of the responseExtensions in a response. In both, it is identified by the object identifier id-pkix-ocsp-nonce, and extnValue holds the encoded Nonce value.

If the extension is present, the Nonce MUST be at least 1 octet and can be up to 128 octets. The ASN.1 type is OCTET STRING(SIZE(1..128)). The 1 octet minimum exists for backward compatibility with older OCSP requesters that follow RFC 6960.

The value MUST be generated with a cryptographically strong pseudorandom number generator, as described in RFC 4086.

Implementations compliant with RFC 8954 cannot process nonces larger than its 32 octet limit.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret number goes into the question and comes back in the answer. It has to be at least one digit long and at most a very long number, and it must be picked at random.

sections.title: Rules for Requesters and Responders
sections.content:
An OCSP requester that implements this extension MUST use a Nonce of at least 32 octets.

A responder that supports the Nonce extension MUST accept Nonce lengths from 16 octets up to and including 32 octets. For requests whose Nonce is 1 to 15 octets or 33 to 128 octets, the responder MAY answer without the Nonce extension.

A responder that implements this document MUST reject any request with a Nonce of 0 octets or more than 128 octets, using the malformedRequest OCSPResponseStatus described in Section 4.2.1 of RFC 6960.
sections.plainLanguage: Askers must use a long secret number. Answerers must accept medium-long ones, may skip very short or very long ones, and must refuse an empty or giant one.

sections.title: An Encoded Example
sections.content: The RFC gives a hexadecimal example of an encoded Nonce extension carrying a 32 octet Nonce. The decoded form is a SEQUENCE of 47 octets, containing the ocspNonce object identifier (1 3 6 1 5 5 7 48 1 2) and an OCTET STRING of 34 octets that wraps the inner 32 octet OCTET STRING holding the nonce itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is like a labelled envelope: the label says it holds a nonce, and inside is the long random number.

sections.title: Replay Attacks
sections.content:
Between the moment a certificate's status changes and the moment the previous OCSP response expires, a copy of that old response could be used to claim the certificate is still valid. Including the requester's nonce in the response shows it is the most recent one and not an old copy.

There is a catch. A responder may choose not to send the Nonce extension even when the requester did, as noted in RFC 5019. An on-path attacker could then intercept the request and answer with an earlier response that has no Nonce. The RFC says this can be mitigated by configuring the server to use a short interval between the thisUpdate and nextUpdate fields of the response.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret number proves the answer was made just now. But if the answerer is allowed to leave it out, a sneaky person could hand back an old answer, so answers should go out of date quickly.

sections.title: IANA and the ASN.1 Modules
sections.content:
The appendices replace the entirety of Section 5 of RFC 8954 with updated ASN.1 modules for OCSP. Appendix A.1 is a module in the 1998 ASN.1 syntax and Appendix A.2 is the same content in the 2008 syntax. The 1998 module remains the normative one, per the policy of the PKIX Working Group. The update also addresses Erratum ID 5891.

IANA has assigned two object identifiers in the "SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier" registry: 111 for id-mod-ocsp-2024-88 and 112 for id-mod-ocsp-2024-08.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook for how messages are written down was reissued in two styles, and each got an official catalogue number.
